items.claim: A full product and version banner in a response header is an information-disclosure finding of low severity, not an exploit, because the header alone confers no capability unless a specific matching vulnerability is shown to be reachable.
items.disproof: It escalates when the disclosed version identifies a component with a demonstrated, reachable, unpatched vulnerability on the same host, which turns the banner into a targeting aid rather than the finding itself; it stays informational when no such path is demonstrated and the only effect is that an attacker learns what they are facing.

sources.quote: if you instrument Docker from a web server to provision containers through an API, you should be even more careful than usual with parameter checking

items.body: Mechanism: A full product and version banner in a response header is an information-disclosure finding of low severity, not an exploit, because the header alone confers no capability unless a specific matching vulnerability is shown to be reachable. How to apply it in the field: treat this as the fp_rule it is — a hunter must be able to state the concrete observation that demonstrates it, with a request and response in hand, before the finding is reportable. Boundary of the rule: It escalates when the disclosed version identifies a component with a demonstrated, reachable, unpatched vulnerability on the same host, which turns the banner into a targeting aid rather than the finding itself; it stays informational when no such path is demonstrated and the only effect is that an attacker learns what they are facing.

items.claim: Reaching a container provisioning API is only container escape rather than a mere access-control gap once the request can be shown to start a container with a host filesystem mount or privileged mode, since the sharing feature is what converts API access into host impact.
items.disproof: It IS host compromise when a request creates a container that shares the host root or mounts the host directory, because the container can then alter the host filesystem; it is NOT escape when the API only permits listing or starting unprivileged isolated containers, where the impact stays inside the container boundary and the correct finding is unauthorised API access.

sources.quote: Docker allows you to share a directory between the Docker host and a guest container; and it allows you to do so without limiting the access rights of the container.

items.claim: A workload misconfiguration finding must be proved by the effective runtime configuration, not by the manifest alone, because whether host namespaces are actually shared is what the control is stated to disallow.
items.disproof: The finding holds when the effective spec sets the host-namespace flags or a privileged container context and that is what runs; it is void when the manifest requests it but a policy or admission controller rewrites the effective spec before it runs, in which case the observable configuration is compliant and the manifest alone proves nothing.

sources.quote: Sharing the host namespaces must be disallowed.
Docker allows you to share a directory between the Docker host and a guest container; and it allows you to do so without limiting the access rights of the container.

items.claim: Mounting the container runtime control socket into an application container nullifies the rest of the hardening around it, because the socket grants the same authority as the daemon and the shared-directory primitive is reachable through it.
items.disproof: It is a genuine bypass when the application process can reach the socket and issue provisioning calls, since that restores daemon-equivalent privilege; it is not when the socket is present but unreachable to the untrusted process, the runtime runs rootless, or a proxy mediates the API with its own authorisation — in those cases the daemon privilege is not actually delegated.

items.claim: A workload running under the open-ended permissive security profile is not a defect on its own, because that profile is defined as entirely unrestricted and is intended for infrastructure workloads managed by trusted users; the report must identify what the openness actually exposes.
items.disproof: It IS a finding when the permissive profile applies to a workload reachable by untrusted input, for example one exposed through an application API; it is NOT a finding when the workload is genuinely infrastructure managed by privileged trusted operators, in which case the permissive profile is the documented intent and reporting it is noise.
